objectives: LO 2.1.1: Know bond terms, issuer types (Treasury, agency, muni, corporate, foreign), their tax treatment and the risks bonds carry
LO 2.2.1: Calculate a convertible's conversion ratio and value, investment value, both premiums and downside risk
LO 2.3.1: Analyze immunization, ladders, barbells, bullets and the five bond swaps
LO 2.3.2: Match fixed-income choices to an investor's goals, taxes, horizon and rate outlook
LO 2.4.1: Read yield curve shapes, the three term-structure theories and what each curve implies for buying bonds
LO 2.5.1: Recognize preferred stock features, how it compares with bonds and how to value it
synthesis: Bonds are the stability and income engine of most client portfolios, so this module feeds asset allocation (Module 6), bond pricing, duration and yield math (Modules 4 and 7) and tax-aware account placement. Knowing which issuer, structure and maturity fits a client's bracket, horizon and rate outlook is the core of a fixed-income recommendation, and convertibles and preferreds bridge into equity analysis.

example.title: Convertible bond: five numbers from one set of facts
example.html:
$1,000 par, 4% semiannual coupon, 10 years left, straight bonds yield 6%, conversion price $62.50, stock $55, convertible priced at $1,000.

  • Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ $62.50 = 16 shares
  • Conversion value = 16 × $55 = $880
  • Investment value: N 20, I/YR 3, PMT $20, FV $1,000 → $851.23
  • Floor = greater of $851.23 and $880 = $880
  • Conversion premium = $120 ÷ $880 = 13.64%
  • Investment premium = $148.77 ÷ $851.23 = 17.48%
  • Downside risk = $148.77 ÷ $1,000 = 14.88%

keyNumbers: >10% private use; qualified if 95%+ for qualified purposes (2026 edition figure)
$25–$10,000; 12-month hold; 3-month penalty within 5 years (2026 edition figure)
mustKnow: TEY = tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − t); after-tax yield = taxable yield × (1 − t)
Convertible: ratio = par ÷ conversion price; CV = ratio × stock price; floor = greater of IV or CV
Downside risk % divides by market price; investment premium % divides by investment value
Immunization: portfolio duration = time horizon; rebalance as duration drifts
Only liquidity preference theory is limited to an upward-sloping curve
Treasuries: no state/local tax; agencies: taxable at all levels; GNMA has the direct guarantee
Preferred: V = D ÷ r; dividend is % of par, paid quarterly; cumulative arrears come first
traps: Treasuries are default-risk free, not risk free
Zeros and STRIPS create phantom income in taxable accounts
Eurobonds can be in any currency; Yankee bonds remove currency risk
With an inverted curve, the textbook favors call-protected long bonds
A barbell is active; a ladder is the passive, staggered one
tips: Convertible questions: write CV, IV and price in a row before computing any %
With state tax in a muni problem, tax each bond only where it is actually taxed
Low coupon + long maturity + low YTM = biggest price swings
